text:
There's a line in Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians that Peter Thiel keeps coming back to: "For when they shall say, Peace and safety; then sudden destruction cometh upon them." In his lectures on the Antichrist, which he's now given in San Francisco, Rome and Nashville, he treats "peace and safety" as the slogan the Antichrist will run on. I've been thinking about that for a long time, because if you take the theology out, what's left is a serious claim about technology and power: in a frightened world, the most dangerous person is the one who promises to keep it safe.

The reasoning goes like this. Every few decades there's a new way the world might end. After 1945 it was nuclear war, later it was climate change and pandemics, and now it's AI. Each one comes with the same offer: give someone enough authority and the disaster can be prevented. Thiel calls this the choice between "Antichrist or Armageddon," and his point is that we treat the first option as if it costs nothing.

It's worth asking what that authority would actually need. A technology that's banned in every country but one hasn't been banned. To really stop something, you'd need a power that reaches every country, knows about every weapons program and can see what every large computer is running. However good its intentions, that's a world government with nothing outside its reach, and I don't see how it avoids becoming totalitarian.

What makes this hard to dismiss is that Thiel doesn't have to imagine that government. Some of the people most worried about AI have already described it. In 2019 the philosopher Nick Bostrom wrote a paper called "The Vulnerable World Hypothesis," arguing that if some future technology turned out to be cheap and destructive enough, surviving it might require near-total surveillance, a "high-tech panopticon," along with effective global governance. He wasn't hoping for it. He was saying it might be the price. Eliezer Yudkowsky went further in a 2023 piece in Time, calling for a worldwide halt to training large AI models, tracking of the chips they run on, and a willingness to bomb datacenters that refused to comply.

Thiel has called Yudkowsky, Bostrom and Greta Thunberg "legionnaires of the Antichrist." I think that's unfair to them. They're afraid of real things, and some of those things deserve fear. But the question he's pointing at is fair, and the people asking for a global pause rarely answer it: who holds the off switch, and what stops them from using it for everything else?

Yudkowsky matters to Thiel for another reason too. In the late '90s, he was one of the most optimistic people anywhere about superintelligence, which he hoped would cure aging and eventually death. In 2000 he co-founded the institute that's now called MIRI, and Thiel was one of its biggest early donors. His latest book is titled If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies, and Thiel says he's embarrassed he ever funded him. For Thiel, that turn, from expecting technology to defeat death to expecting it to kill everyone, is what happened to the whole culture, and it's the fear that makes "peace and safety" sound reasonable.

It also explains why Thiel sees no conflict between his faith and his interest in longevity, which he's funded for years. The usual objection is that wanting to live forever is a kind of rebellion against God, but in his reading the Bible is on the other side. Christianity doesn't promise a soul drifting off to heaven. That's closer to Plato. It promises a body raised from the dead, in a world where nobody dies. Paul calls death "the last enemy." In Matthew 10, among the instructions Jesus gives the twelve is "raise the dead," and in Acts both Peter and Paul do it. On this point I think he's right. Whatever you make of the longevity project, it isn't obviously un-Christian.

Seen that way, science had a destination, and Thiel thinks it has lost sight of it. Francis Bacon, who did more than anyone to found the experimental method, wrote a whole book on prolonging human life. Today a growing number of countries, Canada among them, let doctors help patients die. That's a harder subject than Thiel allows it to be, and it shouldn't be reduced to a talking point, but the change in direction is real.

Underneath all of this is a bigger claim: that science is a Christian inheritance in the first place. Part of the argument is about time. Much of the ancient world thought history repeats itself. The Stoics believed the universe burns up and is rebuilt, the same every time, and if that's how things work, there's little reason to try to improve anything. Scripture tells a story with a start and an end, and the end is better. Daniel 12:4 says "many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased," and Bacon printed that verse on the title page of his 1620 book on the new method. Thiel calls Daniel "the first true historian."

The other part comes from René Girard, Thiel's teacher at Stanford. Girard thought people copy each other's desires, become rivals because of it, and restore peace by uniting against a scapegoat whose guilt everyone takes for granted. In his reading, the Gospels are the first story told from the scapegoat's side, insisting the victim was innocent, and that makes the old mechanism harder to run. Thiel's example is the witch trials. Two of their most important early critics were believers. The physician Johann Weyer wrote in 1563 that the accused women were mostly sick and confused. The Jesuit Friedrich Spee argued in 1631 that torture would get a confession out of anyone, and that many of the condemned were innocent. If no witch spoiled the harvest, then something else did, and finding out what is the work of science.

This is the strongest historical part of his case, though it isn't as clean as he presents it. The trials were run by Christians of both churches, and Weyer and Spee were arguing against their own. Greek and Islamic scholars did serious science long before Europe's Scientific Revolution. Christianity produced both the persecution and the arguments that ended it, which Girard would probably say is the whole point.

As for who the Antichrist might be, Thiel won't name anyone. In Nashville he said "I don't think I'm the Antichrist," and he doesn't expect a tech billionaire either. His guess is a charismatic politician aiming for the American presidency. He also kept returning to the age of 33, when Alexander the Great died after conquering most of the known world, and roughly when Jesus died, to show how much a single life can change in a short time. Alexander needed armies. Someone who inherits a surveillance system built for our safety wouldn't.

Is anything holding that back? In his second letter to the Thessalonians, Paul says the "man of lawlessness" can't come until whatever restrains him is "taken out of the way." The Greek word is katechon, and Paul never says what it is. Early writers like Tertullian thought it was Rome, and in the 20th century the German legal theorist Carl Schmitt revived the idea. Thiel's candidate, in a lecture titled "New Rome," is the United States, the only country with the ideology, the military and the financial reach of an empire. "When the US is done," he said, "the West is done, and the world is done."

The twist that follows is the most interesting part of the whole series. Anything strong enough to restrain the Antichrist is strong enough to become him, and if a one-world state ever comes, the likeliest source is the one country that already reaches everywhere. Thiel called America "ground zero of the one-world state" and "ground zero of the resistance to the one-world state." The protector and the threat could be the same system, with a different person in charge.

There are real problems with all of this. The biggest is that the theory can't lose. Any new AI regulation can be read as a step toward the world state, and any warning about risk as the Antichrist's slogan, so nothing that happens could show him he's wrong. The Nashville Scene's reviewer complained that across about six hours, he gave very few specifics. And it matters who's talking. Thiel co-founded Palantir, which sells data software to governments, militaries and intelligence agencies, and he has a lot of money riding on AI. That doesn't make the warning wrong, but it's a reason to read it carefully.

Thiel likes to ask founders what important truth very few people agree with them on. His own answer seems to be that the catastrophe isn't the only thing to fear, and that whoever offers to save us from it may be worse. I'm not sure it needs the Antichrist to be true. AI can be dangerous, and the people saying so aren't crazy. But it's much easier to picture the world ending in a dramatic disaster than ending quietly, with everyone agreeing it was for their own safety, and the second picture is the one Thiel wants people to see.

text:
When you're trying to break a habit, the craving is only part of the problem. The other part is the thinking that won't stop around it.

You go over the last relapse again and again, and you argue with yourself about whether one more time would really matter.

Psychologists call this rumination, which means going over the same thoughts again and again without getting anywhere. For a lot of people, the habit was the fastest way to switch that noise off, and that's what turns rumination into a trigger.

A study from Stanford looked at what turns it down.

In 2015, a team led by Gregory Bratman sent 38 people who lived in cities on a 90-minute walk. Half of them walked through quiet parkland with grass and trees, and the other half walked along a busy road. The people who walked in nature said they were going over the same thoughts less afterwards. Brain scans showed less activity in an area at the front of the brain called the subgenual prefrontal cortex, which tends to be more active when people are stuck on sad or worrying thoughts. The people who walked by the road didn't show either change.

Both groups walked for the same time and got the same exercise, so the difference came from where they walked.

Now think about where your rumination usually happens. You're on the couch or in bed with your phone in your hand, indoors and sitting still, going over the same thoughts. The longer it goes on, the louder the craving gets, and the habit offers you a quick way out of your own head.

A walk outside is another way out, and it doesn't cost you anything.

This was a small study, with healthy people who weren't trying to stop anything, so it doesn't prove that a walk will stop a craving. What it does show is that where you spend your time can change how much your mind keeps circling the same thing.

So what do we do about it in my program?

In phase 1, before clients have even stopped the habit, one of the daily non-negotiables is what we call an introspection walk. It's 8,000 to 10,000 steps a day, with at least half of it while the sun is out, because daylight also helps set your body clock for sleep.

The walk is time to think. You take whatever is going around in your head and work through it while you move, instead of sitting with it on the couch. It also gets you out of the house during the hours when boredom would usually set in, and boredom is one of the biggest triggers there is.

We put it in early on purpose. By the time clients stop the habit, the walk is already part of their day, so when the thinking starts, they already have somewhere to take it.

None of this makes cravings go away by itself. But it gives your mind a way to settle down that isn't the habit.

This is how you get out of your own head without the habit.

週明けの米株式市場は、AnthropicのS-1正式提出を好感してSOX指数が2.8%急反発したほか、メガテックの資本政策と企業再編を巡る大ニュースが相次ぎました。WSJ・MarketWatchの報道から、今後の投資判断に直結する3つの地殻変動を紹介します。

1. Anthropicの公式S-1提出が照らす「AI経済圏の光と影」

先週の観測報道を経てAnthropicが正式に上場申請を行いました。
急激な売上拡大が確認されたことで市場のAIセンチメントは一旦持ち直しましたが、本質的な論点は「未曾有の計算コスト負担」と「長期利益信託（Long-Term Benefit Trust）による株主統治の制約」にあります。上場を通じて巨額の外部資金を公募市場から調達する道筋がついたものの、投資家がこのビジネスモデルにどれほどのマルチプルを許容するかが、今後のハイテクバリュエーションの新たな基準値となります。

2. Metaの「950億ドル調達」と半導体ベンダー出資の共生関係

Metaが発表した最大950億ドルの資金調達計画において、NvidiaやAMD、Broadcomが株式を引き受ける可能性が浮上した点は極めて象徴的です。
「GPUを売る半導体巨頭が、最大の顧客であるハイパースケーラーの増資を引き受け、その資金で再びGPUを買わせる」というベンダーファイナンス的な資本の循環構造が形成されつつあります。AIインフラの拡張がメガテック単独のバランスシートを超え、サプライチェーン全体の相互依存・共同戦線へと移行している証左です。

If I have to choose one of them it is clearly $AMZN by a wide margin because only $AMZN have a business which is the Everything Store which has a massive moat of the warehouse and shipment network, brand loyalty, and millions of customers who use the established business to buy a broad range of physical items in multiple countries. Their business won't go away if the world is flooded with free open weight models or if new technology developments make LLMs need 100 times less compute, or if AI replaces all apps. Note that if high inflation drives up prices of goods generally, then Amazon's cut of sales revenues goes up with in line with the inflated prices. Counter argument is that a deep recession would cause people to cut back on purchases to only buy necessities (which affects almost every company).

Second choice would be Microsoft because they are so deeply embedded in every medium to large corporation on the planet, every law firm, every accounting firm. Also my impression (which might be out of date) is that Microsoft have been quite savvy to get AI technology from their OpenAI relationship without over the top massive expenditure that OpenAI has exposed itself to. If open weight models kill OpenAI and Anthropic then Microsoft will still do well, because they can offer AI integration to their existing corporate clients (Microsoft systems are full of corporate data, so Microsoft are well positioned to offer AI services that use that corporate data, and Microsoft don't care where the models come from so long as they work).

If I don't have to choose one of them, I probably want to shelter my cash during the coming AI bubble collapse far from tech in oil, other energy, consumer staples (Nestle and similar), and companies that have tollbooth businesses with moats where their income will track the coming massive inflation (e.g. VISA, Mastercard).

I want to own companies that:
(A) Sell something that everyone needs to use, or will never give up using, like their smartphone or their electronic payments network, or food, or shelter, or energy for transport and home heating / cooling, or healthcare, or in the USA their car. Note that smartphone is not optional as it is required for biometric identity verification to access banking, but people can keep their Smartphone much longer on average before replacement.
(B) Sell something that can't be printed or created by AI or government (so I don't want publishing, films, music, or fiat currency)
(C) Have an internationally diverse business income
(D) Have a moat
(E) Will do well in the face of massive inflation, so needs to have pricing power or naturally follows inflation because they take a cut of a flow of money.
(F) Will survive a deep recession.

An obvous sector that will suffer badly is airlines as they are so dependent on the price of jet fuel, and energy prices are going to go up due to destruction of refineries and other energy infrastructure in Russia and in Middle Eastern nations. I predict that air travel will return to the 1970s model where only a "jet set" of wealthy people can afford to fly.

This is crazy. Absolutely insane.

We were told the AI boom would create a massive wave of new tech jobs. Instead, Microsoft just offered voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees, nearly 27% of its entire workforce.

I know this isn't a mandatory layoff, but it's a clear sign of how much cash the AI infrastructure race is burning. Building data centers for OpenAI, Anthropic and cloud customers is so expensive that Microsoft is actively trying to shrink its payroll to protect cash flow.

Ironically, even the teams building Copilot and AI Experiences are on the buyout list.

- Scope: Around 60,000 employees out of 223,000 globally are eligible across the US, India, UK, and Canada.
- Seniority: Open to Level 70 and below.
- Who's included: AI Experiences, Copilot, Xbox, Windows + Devices, Finance, and HR. Sales, Marketing, and Security are excluded.
- The package: Standard severance, with a minimum of 60 days of base pay on payroll, scaling up to 39 weeks of base pay depending on level and tenure.
- Timeline: Employees must decide by early December, with their last day set for December 31.

text:
Kalshi just became the NBA's official prediction market partner.

We went through the court records, regulator filings and Kalshi's own statements. 

Here's what this announcement left out:

1/
The deal makes Kalshi a "Preferred Prediction Market Exchange of the NBA."
Kalshi gets NBA logos, marketing rights and official league data to settle its NBA markets. Polymarket got the same deal.
2/
Here's what makes it strange.
In May 2025, after Kalshi started offering spreads and moneylines on NBA games, an NBA lawyer wrote to federal regulators asking for protections against the integrity risks of prediction markets.
17 months later, Kalshi is a partner.
3/
The NBA has reason to worry.
Former Raptor Jontay Porter admitted he left games early to help bettors who bet the "under" on his stats. He pleaded guilty to federal wire fraud conspiracy and was banned for life.
4/
In October 2025, the FBI arrested Terry Rozier in a case centered on a March 2023 game he left after less than 10 minutes. Sportsbooks had flagged suspicious betting on his stats.
The NBA reviewed that game in 2023 and found no rule violation.
Rozier has pleaded not guilty. His trial is set for February 2027.
5/
To be clear, those bets ran through sportsbooks, not Kalshi.
But they show where the risk is: inside information about who plays and who's hurt.
6/
Kalshi listed markets on exactly that.
It offered contracts on athlete injuries, including how long players would be sidelined and whether specific NFL players would suit up for Week 1.
Kalshi has since pulled them.
7/
Then there's Giannis Antetokounmpo.
He became a Kalshi shareholder in a deal signed on NBA trade deadline day. Earlier that week, Kalshi listed markets on where he'd be traded.
Kalshi says the deal wasn't in place while those markets ran, his stake is under 1%, and he's barred from trading NBA markets.
8/
Kalshi says it isn't a sportsbook.
But its ads promoted sports betting as legal in all 50 states. And according to a federal appeals court, sports made up 95% of its 2025 revenue.
In August, that court ruled 3-0 that Kalshi's sports contracts are, in substance, sports gambling.
9/
In most states you must be 21 to bet on the NBA at a sportsbook. On Kalshi, it's 18.
CNN estimates 18-to-21-year-olds traded $5.4 billion on Kalshi so far this year. Kalshi has also recruited "ambassadors" on college campuses.
10/
Sportsbooks let problem gamblers ban themselves through state self-exclusion programs.
A Massachusetts man who had self-excluded says in a lawsuit that Kalshi offered no such option, and that he lost tens of thousands of dollars there in one month.
11/
Kalshi's ads said "We aren't the house."
But Kalshi owns a trading company, Kalshi Trading, that takes the other side of some customer bets.
And Bloomberg reported that Jump Trading agreed to take an equity stake in Kalshi in exchange for trading on the platform.
12/
So who wins?
Kalshi's own data: over 70% of traders lost money over six months.
Over the long run, traders and analysts surveyed by How Gambling Works estimate only 2–5% of users come out ahead.
13/
Then there's the fine print.
Traders put more than $54 million on whether Iran's Supreme Leader would be "out." When he died, Kalshi paid at the last price before his death, about 40¢ instead of $1, citing a rule about death.
It refunded fees and net losses. Traders sued anyway.
14/
In January, Kalshi didn't pay winners on some NFL season markets.
It paid them after users complained publicly.

@Matthew24906171 @KalishJr @James_Hawke1 @NardMyWally 
one of the best flat earth photos I’ve ever taken. From Criterion Summit Mountain identifier. 

Criterion Summit (Wasco County, Oregon) is the mountain pass and roadside viewpoint on U.S. Route 197 south of Maupin (about 7 miles north of the US 197/US 97 junction). Elevation is roughly 3,360 ft (1,020–1,025 m). It is near the historic unincorporated community of Criterion. 
A sign and viewpoint map (sometimes called a “mountain finder”) mark the summit and identify Cascade Range peaks visible on clear days, ranging from Broken Top to the southwest through peaks such as the Sisters and Mount Jefferson to Mount Adams to the northwest. Local sources also note views of Mount Hood. 
Approximate straight-line distances to major Cascade peaks
These are calculated from the summit’s coordinates (~44.98°N, 120.99°W):
•  Mount Hood (~11,249 ft): ~44 miles
•  Mount Jefferson (~10,500 ft): ~45 miles
•  Broken Top / South Sister area (~9,000–10,360 ft): ~71–72 miles
•  Mount Adams (~12,276 ft): ~88 miles
Visibility depends on clear weather; the open high-desert setting helps with long-distance views.
Nearby local summits/peaks (examples)
From peak databases and topo sources around Criterion Summit:
•  Shaniko Butte: ~17.7 miles
•  Nachter Butte: ~17.8 miles
•  Sugarloaf: ~17.9 miles
•  Cross Hill: ~18.2 miles
•  Friends Peak: ~20 miles
•  Mutton Mountain: ~21 miles
The area also includes the nearby BLM Criterion Tract, which offers open views of the Cascades, the Deschutes River canyon, and local features such as the Mutton Mountains.

FBI releases video of shooter who killed Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University
RESTRICTION: USERS MUST CREDIT “FBI” HANDOUT —EDITORIAL USE ONLY —

SHOTLIST:

UTAH, UNITED STATES (SEPT. 10, 2025) (FBI - RESTRICTED)

1. VARIOUS CCTV FOOTAGE OF SUSPECT JUMPING FROM ROOFTOP OF BUILDING, FLEEING FROM SCENE UTAH, UNITED STATES - SEPT. 10, 2025 - RESTRICTION: USERS MUST CREDIT “FBI” HANDOUT —EDITORIAL USE ONLY — The FBI on Thursday, Sept. 11, released video footage of the shooter involved in the fatal attack at Utah Valley University that left American conservative commentator Charlie Kirk dead.

Authorities said the footage shows the suspect jumping from the rooftop of a building shortly after the September 10 shooting before fleeing the scene. Investigators recovered a firearm and ammunition abandoned in a wooded area near the university.

Trace evidence collected from the rooftop included shoe impressions, a forearm imprint, and a palm print, according to officials.

The FBI released additional photos Thursday of a person of interest tied to the shooting of American conservative commentator Charlie Kirk.

“The FBI continues to work alongside our law enforcement partners to seek justice in the murder of Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University on September 10, 2025. We are releasing additional photos of a person of interest,” the bureau wrote on the US social media company X’s platform.

The four grainy photos appear to depict a college-age male clad in a black long-sleeve t-shirt, jeans, a backpack, a baseball cap and black sunglasses.

This comes as the FBI offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to the arrest of the person who fatally shot Kirk.

"The FBI is offering a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to the identification and arrest of the individual(s) responsible for the murder of Charlie Kirk on September 10, 2025, at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah," the bureau wrote on X.

Earlier Thursday, the bureau released a pair of photos of a "person of interest" in the fatal shooting of the American right-wing commentator, appealing to the public for assistance in identifying the individual.

Kirk, 31, was fatally shot Wednesday while addressing a group of students at Utah Valley University in the city of Orem, some 40 miles (64.4 kilometers) south of Salt Lake City. The apparent targeted attack occurred despite security, including six university police officers and Kirk's private team.

Online videos captured the moment a bullet struck Kirk as he spoke, sending students fleeing in panic. He was rushed to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead hours later.

The FBI said investigators found a "high-powered bolt-action rifle" that was recovered in a wooded area linked to the suspected shooter's escape route.

Multiple media reports suggested that ammunition engraved with "transgender and antifascist ideology" was found in the rifle. The reports cited an internal law enforcement document.

The New York Times cited an anonymous senior law enforcement official who stressed that the information had not been verified, did not match other summaries of evidence and may have been misread.

The investigation has so far been able to track the suspect's movements starting roughly 30 minutes before Kirk was shot, Utah Department of Public Safety Commissioner Beau Mason said during a news conference. Authorities believe the suspect arrived near the Utah Valley University campus at 11.52 am local time (1752GMT) and made his way to the roof and to what Robert Bohls, the FBI special agent in charge of the Salt Lake City field office, described as a "shooting location."

After the shooting, the suspect moved to the other side of the building, jumped down and made his way into a nearby neighborhood where investigators have sought home camera surveillance footage.

Two people of interest were taken into custody in the aftermath of the shooting but were later released after being cleared of suspicion. Mason said both faced "threats" after being released and asked the public to be "patient with the investigative process."

"These individuals were not suspects. They were people of interest. We ask that you do not impose into those people and that investigative process. They don't deserve that harassment," said Mason.

text:
That’s a fair criticism, and mathematically, you’re largely correct. My proposal deliberately preserves the Electoral College’s existing state weighting, including the advantage smaller states receive.

I don’t believe any American inherently deserves a more powerful vote because of where they live. That’s a legitimate weakness of the current system that my proposal doesn’t fully eliminate.

What I’m trying to accomplish is proportional representation within each state. A Republican in California or a Democrat in Wyoming would contribute toward their candidate’s national electoral total, even when their preferred candidate loses the state.

I recognize that a national popular vote offers greater equality between individual voters. My concern is preserving some balance between population-based representation and the federal structure, while reducing winner-take-all distortions and the disproportionate attention given to competitive states.

It’s a compromise, and I think it’s worth debating whether that compromise is preferable to either alternative.

Old Flame (Gambler's Folly Book 4) by Mellie Miller is a heartfelt second-chance paranormal shifter romance that blends emotional healing, mature love, and the magic of fate. Billionaire and bear shifter Kort Behrens has been lucky in business but unlucky in love—after two failed marriages and a string of gold diggers, he’s given up hope of finding a real connection. Elizabeth Murphy, a widow for four years, has rebuilt her life through her Reiki practice and the quiet companionship of her cat, Puzzle, still carrying the quiet ache of a long marriage that never fully satisfied her deeper desires. When these old college friends (who never dated) unexpectedly reunite on the way to the enchanted world of Gambler’s Folly, sparks fly and a full-blown romance blooms. Will they seize this second chance at a happily-ever-after, or will doubts and fears snatch it away? On Gambler’s Folly, every love story is a gamble—and Fate always deals the final hand. A slow-burn friends-to-lovers tale full of heart, sensuality, and the series’ signature fantasy charm.

About the author
Mellie Miller first fell in love with writing in a high school creative writing class. Married to her one and only, Steve, they began their journey through life in 1976 and, after two children and many moves, she finally has the time to devote to this love. She mainly writes fantasy romance, often with a paranormal twist, though she also has a short book sharing her struggle with breast cancer. Mellie feels her background in music, martial arts (2nd-degree black belt), and Reiki gives her a broad palette to draw on for her character development. Many of her stories incorporate one or more of these talents. As a lover of fantasy, Mellie hopes the worlds and stories she creates will give others a bit of escape from the hectic world around us and offer hope for a happy outcome. She and her husband live in rural Georgia and share their lives with cats, dogs, and a flock of chickens. She also writes under the pen name Sultonna Nadine.

If Jesus knew Judas was corrupt but allowed him to remain among the Twelve, why should Christians be surprised that sinners exist within the Church today?

Things become more intense when the Catholic caller admits he no longer wants to attend Mass and describes experiencing spiritual peace while praying alone. Through Matthew 13:44-46, Sam Shamoun explains the parables of the pearl of great price and the treasure hidden in the field, connecting them to Jesus Christ, the Catholic Church, the Holy Eucharist, and the sacrifice of the Mass. Sam Shamoun argues that Christians cannot simply reject the Church because of its imperfect members while expecting to enjoy everything Christ offers through His body.

Sam Shamoun then uses Matthew 9:9-13 to explain why the Church is a spiritual hospital for sinners, not a gathering of perfect people. Jesus Christ is the divine physician, and Christians need the Church, its bishops, priests, sacraments, and Christian community for spiritual healing and growth.

Finally, Sam Shamoun examines Hebrews 10:23-25, Hebrews 13:17, Ecclesiastes 4, Proverbs 3, Psalm 133, and John 17 to explain the importance of Christian fellowship, obedience to spiritual authority, unity in the Body of Christ, and why following Jesus in isolation contradicts God's design for His people.

text:
He called me proud. Emily called him controlling. Eventually, he stopped discussing money with me.

Or so I thought.

That night, I walked into the bathroom and called him.

He answered immediately.

“You received it,” he said.

“Why are you sending me forty thousand dollars?”

“Because you have a chance to leave this relationship with your dignity intact.”

“What arrangement are you talking about?”

He sighed impatiently.

“Emily has been seeing someone else. His name is James. Their families have known each other for years, and he is the kind of man who can provide the future she deserves.”

My stomach tightened.

“Are you telling me your daughter is cheating on me?”

“I'm telling you that feelings are complicated. James has offered to marry her, and Emily has been considering it.”

I looked through the bathroom doorway at the woman sleeping in our bed.

“Then why hasn't she told me?”

“Because she doesn't want to hurt you.”

I nearly laughed.

“So your solution is to buy me?”

“My solution is to prevent a humiliating situation for everyone involved.”

I ended the call.

For the next hour, I sat on the bathroom floor, staring at the transfer notification. I wanted to wake Emily and demand answers, but I also wanted to know how much of what her father had said was true.

Eventually, I returned to bed.

She was awake.

“Who were you talking to?” she asked.

“Your father.”

Her expression changed immediately.

“What did he say?”

I showed her the messages.

She covered her mouth, and tears filled her eyes.

“I'm sorry,” she whispered.

Those two words hurt more than anything her father had said.

I asked whether she knew about the money.

She nodded.

“Dad told me he was going to offer you something to leave. I didn't know he would send that much.”

“And James?”

She looked away.

“James and I went on three dates before you and I got engaged. Our families wanted us together, but I didn't feel what I feel for you.”

“Then why is your father telling me you're considering marrying him?”

Emily began crying.

“Because James came back six months ago. He told my father he still wanted me, and Dad started putting pressure on me again. I told him I wasn't interested.”

“Did you tell James that?”

“Yes.”

“Have you seen him since?”

She hesitated.

That hesitation changed the entire conversation.

“Emily, have you seen him since?”

“Twice.”

“Were those business meetings?”

“The first time, yes. The second time, we had dinner.”

I stepped away from her.

She immediately explained that her father had arranged the dinner without telling her James would be there. She claimed she stayed because leaving would have caused a scene.

I asked whether James had tried to kiss her.

She shook her head.

Then she admitted he had held her hand under the table.

“And you let him?”

“I pulled away.”

“After how long?”

She couldn't answer.

I left the bedroom and slept on the sofa.

The following morning, Emily told me everything.

Apparently, James had promised her father that he would buy a house for the couple, pay off a family business loan, and support Emily's mother financially. Richard believed the arrangement would protect the family from financial difficulties.

Emily insisted she had rejected the proposal.

But when I asked why she hadn't told me about the dinner, she said she was afraid I would misunderstand.

I told her that hiding something because your partner might be upset was exactly how misunderstandings became betrayals.

For three days, we barely spoke.

Then James contacted me directly.

He asked to meet at a restaurant.

I went because I wanted to hear what kind of man was willing to negotiate another man's engagement.

James arrived in an expensive car, ordered coffee, and spoke calmly.

“I don't want to fight you,” he said. “Emily deserves to choose her own future.”

“Then why are you trying to marry her?”

“Because I love her.”

“Does she love you?”

He looked down at his cup.

“She loved me once.”

text:
Internal Weather

Some days are really good.

The sun seems to shine just for us.
Truth flows effortlessly,
words find their way home,
and the heart glows with warmth.

Yesterday was one of those days.

And then there are days like today.

I wake beneath a sky I don’t recognize.
My body feels heavy.
My hands forget how to hold things.
I spill stuff and trip over my own feet.

And somewhere along the way,
a storm begins to gather.

A conversation that should have been easy
becomes a series of misunderstandings.
Our frequencies seem mismatched.
Every word I offer in an attempt to clarify
only distorts the meaning further.

Like raindrops falling on newspaper,
trying to wash the newsprint clean,
only to leave the words illegible.

Nothing is particularly wrong.
And yet everything feels wrong.

An inexplicable sense of doom.
A coldness where yesterday there was warmth.
Shivers down my spine,
my skin prickling like an anxious cat
sensing a storm before it arrives.

So which day was real?

Yesterday’s sunshine?
Or today’s darkness?

Maybe both.
Or neither.

Feelings are real.
Only in that they exist. But don’t believe the stories they try to tell.

We don’t question happiness.
We bask in its warmth without demanding proof.
But suffering arrives,
and suddenly we need to interrogate it 
like some detective or prosecutor. 

We question our relationships,
our choices, our entire existence,
Like pain possesses some special authority
to reveal truths that happiness cannot.

But why should it?

Perhaps my body woke up exhausted.
Perhaps hormones shifted.
Perhaps the pressure in the atmosphere changed.
Perhaps a thousand invisible conditions
converged to produce this particular storm.

I have no fucking clue.
And I don’t need to.

Weather be just weathering.

Moisture gathers.
Pressure shifts.
Clouds collide.
Rain falls.

It happens.
And then it passes.

We don’t declare that we shall henceforth
wear rainboots for the rest of our lives
simply because it’s raining today.

Nor should we make permanent declarations
about our lives
based on temporary emotional conditions.

A forecast is not a prophecy.
And forecasts are often wrong.

The sky does not become damaged by a storm.
Nor does it become more complete
when the sun returns.

It just holds space for whatever happens to occur.

So today, I will lay low.

I will resist the urge to explain,
to defend,
to untangle every misunderstanding,
to assign meaning to every uncomfortable feeling.

I will try not to create consequences
that outlast the conditions that produced them.

I will allow myself to feel unwell
without making it someone else’s emergency.

Emotional stability
is not the ability to remain perpetually sunny.
It’s how we handle the bad weather when it inevitably comes.

Yesterday was beautiful.
Today is difficult.

Neither invalidates the other.

And underneath it all,
the sky remains.

So I wait.

Until the storm passes.
Until the newspaper dries.
Until the words become legible again.

And in the meantime,

We apologize for any internal weather-related damages.

text:
Floodwater reached Broad Street at Lockwood in Charleston on Monday. The morning warning was cancelled, but moderate coastal flooding is forecast around Tuesday’s 9:06 a.m. and Wednesday’s 9:57 a.m. high tides.

The coastal flood warning for Charleston and coastal Colleton was cancelled at 10:29 a.m. Monday, 31 minutes before its scheduled end. That cancellation did not end the week’s tidal-flooding threat.

Strong onshore winds combined with exceptionally high astronomical tides to push water toward the coast, leaving coastal roads vulnerable even under sunny skies. Further flooding could disrupt the next two morning commutes, with flood-prone routes potentially impassable until water recedes.

Monday’s warning forecast 1–2 feet of saltwater inundation above ground along shorelines and tidal waterways in Charleston and coastal Colleton. That was a forecast, not a measured street-water depth. The available evidence documents street flooding but does not establish an observed Charleston Harbor peak, confirmed property damage or a verified tally of road closures.

Potentially major flooding was forecast for Monday morning; the evidence does not confirm that major flood stage was reached. Moderate flooding remains the forecast for Tuesday and Wednesday mornings.

Tuesday, October 27’s high tide is at 9:06 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time. Wednesday, October 28’s is at 9:57 a.m. Charleston offers TIDEeye and a city flood-road-closure resource for checking routes. Current road conditions, rather than the end of Monday’s warning, should guide commute decisions.

#CharlestonFlooding #CoastalFlooding
